Birding in Spain

599bird species present
13birding regions
8reserves and parks named
Extremadura Doñana and the Guadalquivir Strait of Gibraltar Sierra de Andújar and the Andalusian sierras Pyrenees Ebro Delta Aragonese and Catalan steppes Gallocanta Picos de Europa and the north coast Albufera Catalan coast La Mancha Granada and Almería
Birds When to Go Where to Bird Itineraries Prep FAQ Community

At a glance

Best months
  • March and April for the steppe leks and Extremadura, late February to April and October to November for Doñana passage, late August to early September for the Tarifa raptor crossing
  • November to February for the Gallocanta cranes
Getting around
A hire car throughout. Distances are long and the good hours are early, so most itineraries base for several nights rather than moving daily
The one thing to know
Summer shuts the middle of the day. August in Monfragüe regularly passes 40 degrees and the birding happens at dawn and dusk or not at all

When to Go

The Spanish birding year is shaped by heat and by two bottlenecks. Spring runs early and hard, from February to May, and then the plains shut down for the summer. Autumn belongs to the Strait of Gibraltar, and winter to the cranes and the lynx.

spring

February to May

The best of the country, and the reason most itineraries run now. Bustards display through March and early April, before the grass grows tall enough to hide them.

Go for Steppe leks, Extremaduran raptors, Doñana on passage, and everything singing.

Trade off Easter pushes prices up, and the good operators fill their April departures a year ahead.

Typical daily average
  • Sevilla: 7 to 26 °C / 45 to 79 °F
  • Cáceres: 5 to 23 °C / 41 to 73 °F
  • Zaragoza: 4 to 23 °C / 39 to 73 °F

summer

June and July

The plains become unworkable and the birding moves uphill. Monfragüe in August is described by the people who guide there as an endurance exercise.

Go for The Pyrenees and the Picos, where Lammergeier and Wallcreeper are on the cliffs and the air is breathable.

Trade off Dawn or nothing in the south, and Doñana's marshes may have dried out altogether.

Typical daily average
  • Sevilla: 17 to 35 °C / 63 to 95 °F
  • Cáceres: 15 to 34 °C / 59 to 93 °F
  • Zaragoza: 15 to 31 °C / 59 to 88 °F

migration

Late August to October

The Strait of Gibraltar takes over. The last week of August and the first ten days of September are the raptor peak.

Go for Honey Buzzard, Egyptian Vulture and Montagu's Harrier crossing in numbers, with Griffon Vulture running later into the autumn.

Trade off A crossing needs the right wind, so the Strait of Gibraltar rewards several days rather than one.

Typical daily average
  • Sevilla: 14 to 34 °C / 57 to 93 °F
  • Cáceres: 12 to 33 °C / 54 to 91 °F
  • Zaragoza: 11 to 31 °C / 52 to 88 °F

winter

November to January

Cranes fill Gallocanta and the lynx becomes findable, with short coats and thin cover.

Go for Eighty per cent of the western Common Crane population passing one lake, plus wintering wildfowl and the easiest raptor watching of the year.

Trade off Short days, cold mornings on the steppe, and some mountain roads closed.

Typical daily average
  • Sevilla: 6 to 20 °C / 43 to 68 °F
  • Cáceres: 4 to 16 °C / 39 to 61 °F
  • Zaragoza: 3 to 15 °C / 37 to 59 °F

Colours match each region. Select a marker to open its entry below.

One pin per region, and the parks and stops inside each region card carry their own coordinates. The meseta in the middle of the map is high, flat and dry, and the wetland regions ring it at the coasts, which is the shape of most Spanish itineraries.

Granada and Almería

Almería (LEI), Cabo de Gata, the Tabernas desert, Sierra Nevada, Granada (GRX) out

Three days on the driest ground in Europe give Trumpeter Finch, Dupont's Lark and the salt pan flocks. The road out of Granada then climbs to the alpine tops for Alpine Accentor and Citril Finch.

Extremadura, Monfragüe and the Cáceres steppes

Dehesa oak parkland, quartzite ridges and cereal steppe, holding the two largest Cinereous Vulture colonies in Europe

The region operators call the best birding in western Europe, with twenty breeding raptor species. Monfragüe holds 376 pairs of Cinereous Vulture and the Sierra de San Pedro 461, which between them are Europe's two most important colonies.

  • Habitat: Mixed oak forest with a Cistus understorey on quartzite ridges, cut by the Tajo and Tiétar gorges, with dehesa and open steppe on the plains behind.
  • When: April and May, when the Black Vultures and Black Storks are visible on their nests. Eagle Owls call from December to February and show at dusk from the Salto del Gitano viewpoint.
  • Getting there: Plasencia lies 20 km north of the park and Trujillo 60 km south. The visitor centre at Villarreal de San Carlos sits on the road through the middle.
  • Look for: Cinereous Vulture, Spanish Imperial Eagle, Black Stork, Eurasian Eagle-Owl, Great Bustard, Little Bustard, Black-winged Kite, Iberian Magpie
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Nacional de Monfragüe, Reserva Ornitológica de Sierra de Fuentes (SEO/BirdLife reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : Quartzite crags above the Tagus. They hold the densest breeding raptor community in Europe, and Cinereous Vulture, Spanish Imperial Eagle and Black Stork all use one rock face.
    • : The one hamlet inside the park. It holds the centre and the car park for the Salto del Gitano crag, where the vultures nest at eye level across the river.
    • : A walled hill town whose church towers and bullring hold Lesser Kestrel and Pallid Swift. Most visitors work the steppes from here.
    • : Open cereal steppe east of Trujillo, and the ground for Great Bustard, Little Bustard and Pin-tailed Sandgrouse.
    • : A warm-water reservoir with reed-fringed arms and a public hide circuit. Purple Swamphen and Little Bittern stay year round.
    • : The vast dry pseudo-steppe of eastern Badajoz, and the largest single block of bustard habitat in Spain.
  • Also covers: Arrocampo Reservoir, Belén plains, Cáceres, La Serena, Monfragüe National Park, Parque Nacional de Monfragüe, Reserva Ornitológica de Sierra de Fuentes, Trujillo, Villarreal de San Carlos
  • Also watch for: Red Deer and Wild Boar are everywhere in the dehesa, open oak parkland grazed beneath cork and holm oak,, Egyptian Mongoose crosses the tracks in daylight, and Eurasian Otter works the Tajo and the Tiétar below the Salto del Gitano.

Doñana and the Guadalquivir

Atlantic marsh, moving dune and umbrella pine at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, entered on a guided vehicle

Atlantic marsh, dune and pine, and the classic Spanish wetland. Spanish Imperial Eagle, Crested Coot and the marsh assemblage live here, and a guided vehicle is the way in rather than free access.

  • Habitat: Seasonally flooded marisma behind a 35 km sand bar, with stone pine woodland, dune systems and cork oak stands carrying the heronries.
  • When: October to May, while the marisma holds water. Summer combines the lowest levels with the beach crowds at Matalascañas, and 2005, 2012 and 2017 were exceptionally dry years.
  • Getting there: El Rocío is the base, on the A-483 an hour southwest of Seville. The Mazagón road off the A-494 opens the pine woodland and the sandy tracks on the western edge.
  • Look for: Red-knobbed Coot, Marbled Duck, Purple Swamphen, Greater Flamingo, Squacco Heron, Glossy Ibis, Red-crested Pochard, Slender-billed Gull
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Nacional de Doñana, Parque Natural de Doñana (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : A sand-street pilgrimage village on the marsh edge. Its lagoon is watched from the promenade and is the easiest wetland in the park.
    • : Working saltpans on the river's south bank, and the wader roost that fills as the estuary covers.
    • : A tidal estuary and saltpan complex at Huelva. It holds the largest Spoonbill colony in Spain.
    • : A lagoon and cork oak dehesa on the marsh's northern edge, with a large White Stork colony in the trees.
    • Laguna de Medina : A shallow endorheic lagoon outside Jerez, reliable for White-headed Duck and Crested Coot.
  • Visitor centres: El Acebuche visitor centre, La Rocina visitor centre
  • Also covers: Bonanza saltpans, Dehesa de Abajo, El Acebuche visitor centre, El Rocina, El Rocío, La Rocina visitor centre, Laguna de Medina, Madre de las Marismas, Odiel Marshes, Parque Nacional de Doñana, Parque Natural de Doñana
  • Also watch for: Doñana is one of the two places Iberian Lynx never disappeared from, and the guided vehicle routes are how most people see one. Red Deer, Fallow Deer and Wild Boar use the marsh edge, and Egyptian Mongoose is common in the scrub.

The Strait of Gibraltar

The shortest crossing to Africa, fourteen kilometres wide, where every soaring bird in western Europe funnels to a point

Europe's premier bottleneck for soaring birds and the shortest Mediterranean crossing. Roughly 300,000 raptors of about thirty species and 150,000 storks pass each season.

  • Habitat: Rolling open hillside above the strait, broken by rocky gullies and outcrops, with pine and corkwood stands where crossing raptors rest.
  • When: February to May and August to November for the raptor and stork crossings, and something moves across on very nearly every day of the year.
  • Getting there: Tarifa sits on the N-340, 40 km west of Algeciras. Alto del Cabrito is a dirt road north off the N-340 at km 91; the Mirador del Estrecho fills with coach traffic.
  • Look for: Black Kite, Short-toed Snake Eagle, Booted Eagle, European Honey Buzzard, White Stork, Egyptian Vulture, Rüppell's Vulture, Northern Bald Ibis
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural del Estrecho (natural park), Parque Natural Los Alcornocales (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : The southernmost town in mainland Europe, on a strait fourteen kilometres wide. It is the funnel every soaring migrant uses between Africa and Iberia.
    • : The raptor watchpoint on the ridge above the town, staffed through the autumn passage. It is the standard place to count the crossing.
    • : Drained lake bed turned rice and cotton, now the richest raptor and crane ground in the province. Follow its farm tracks.
    • : The saltpans and tidal flats north of Tarifa. Caspian Tern, Osprey and the wintering waders use them.
  • Also covers: Algeciras, Bay of Cádiz, Cazalla observatory, La Janda, Parque Natural del Estrecho, Parque Natural Los Alcornocales, Tarifa
  • Also watch for: The same water carries Common Dolphin, Striped Dolphin and Long-finned Pilot Whale year round, with Orca following the bluefin tuna through July and August. Barbary Macaque holds the upper Rock at Gibraltar itself.

Sierra de Andújar and the Andalusian sierras

Sierra Morena granite and pine above the Jándula reservoir, holding the densest Iberian Lynx population left

The Iberian Lynx stronghold, which several operators now name in the tour title itself, alongside Spanish Imperial Eagle, Black Vulture and Iberian Magpie. Grazalema holds over 700 pairs of Griffon Vulture.

  • Habitat: One of the best-preserved expanses of Mediterranean forest left in Spain: cork, holm and Lusitanian oak over scrub, with riparian woodland along the Río de las Yeguas.
  • When: March to July for the birds. Lynx are easiest between September and December once the ground cover has gone. Winter brings real cold and occasional heavy snow.
  • Getting there: The A-6177 runs north from Andújar on the A-4. The Viñas de Peñallana visitor centre is at km 13, and the Encinarejo track leaves at km 22 over the Jándula bridge.
  • Look for: Griffon Vulture, Black Wheatear, Blue Rock Thrush, Rock Bunting, Thekla's Lark, Red-billed Chough, Alpine Swift
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Natural Sierra de Andújar (natural park), Parque Natural Sierra de Cardeña y Montoro (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : Granite hills of holm oak and cistus in the Sierra Morena. It is the best remaining Iberian Lynx ground and a stronghold for Spanish Imperial Eagle.
    • : The reservoir at the end of the park road. Drive its last kilometres slowly at dawn for lynx and for Black Vulture coming off the roost.
    • : The wettest place in Spain, limestone with relict fir forest. Griffon Vulture gather in numbers and Bonelli's Eagle hold the gorges.
    • : A karst plateau of weathered limestone above Antequera, with Black Wheatear, Blue Rock Thrush and Alpine Swift.
    • Ronda and the Serrania : Limestone gorge and dehesa around the town, with griffon and Bonelli's Eagle over the Tajo.
  • Also covers: El Torcal, Embalse del Jándula, Parque Natural Sierra de Andújar, Parque Natural Sierra de Cardeña y Montoro, Ronda and the Serrania, Sierra de Grazalema
  • Also watch for: This is the Sierra Morena lynx stronghold. Watch from the roadside above the Jándula at dawn and dusk. Red Deer, Wild Boar and Mouflon share the ground, and Spanish Ibex works the crags at Grazalema and El Torcal.

The Pyrenees

Limestone cirques at Ordesa, the conglomerate towers of Riglos, and the highest ground on the northern frontier

Lammergeier and Wallcreeper on the cliffs. The Pyrenees hold 209 territorial Bearded Vulture units, 151 of them in Spain.

  • Habitat: Beech, silver fir and pine climbing into alpine pasture and limestone cirque, with the Ordesa canyon cut a thousand metres below Monte Perdido.
  • When: May and June are the productive months. Snow blocks the roads into spring, and the Ordesa and Añisclo valleys fill on summer weekends and public holidays.
  • Getting there: The Ordesa valley entrance is at Torla, an hour north of Sabiñánigo on the N-260. The El Parador visitor centre opens daily from April to October and holds the main car park.
  • Look for: Bearded Vulture, Wallcreeper, White-winged Snowfinch, Alpine Accentor, Rock Ptarmigan, Citril Finch, Black Woodpecker, Common Rock Thrush
  • National parks: Parque Nacional de Ordesa y Monte Perdido, Parque Nacional de Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici
  • Stops:
    • : A glacial canyon under the range's highest limestone, walked from Torla. Lammergeier, Wallcreeper and Alpine Accentor hold it.
    • : Conglomerate towers rising straight off the plain at the range's southern foot, with a Griffon Vulture colony on the faces.
    • : A quiet western valley of beech and pine below the frontier ridge. Search it for Black Woodpecker, Citril Finch and Lammergeier.
    • : The stone village at the head of the neighbouring valley. The road climbs to high pasture for Rock Thrush and Snowfinch.
    • Sierra de Guara : A pre-Pyrenean limestone massif north of Huesca, cut by canyons. It holds one of the largest griffon vulture concentrations in Spain.
  • Also covers: Ansó, Hecho valley, Mallos de Riglos, Parque Nacional de Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici, Parque Nacional de Ordesa y Monte Perdido, Sierra de Guara
  • Also watch for: Pyrenean Chamois is constant on the high meadows and Alpine Marmot whistles from the scree. Brown Bear holds a small reintroduced population in the central range, and Pyrenean Desman lives in the fastest of the streams.

The Ebro Delta

A Mediterranean delta of rice paddy, lagoon and sand spit, pushed twenty kilometres out from the coastline

A Mediterranean delta rated among the best wetlands in Europe. Audouin's Gull, Greater Flamingo, Slender-billed Gull and the reedbed herons.

  • Habitat: Rice paddy, natural lagoon and working saltpan across a delta reaching 20 km into the Mediterranean, with dune and beach along the two spits.
  • When: January to March gives the driest paddies and concentrates the birds on the lagoons and saltpans. Heat haze is the limit in warm weather, and mosquitoes bite in September.
  • Getting there: Deltebre and Sant Carles de la Ràpita are the two bases, off the AP-7 two hours south of Barcelona. SEO/BirdLife's Riet Vell reserve is at km 18.5 on the Eucaliptus road.
  • Look for: Audouin's Gull, Purple Heron, Eurasian Bittern, Collared Pratincole, Kentish Plover, Moustached Warbler, Whiskered Tern
  • Parks and reserves: Parc Natural del Delta de l'Ebre (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : The delta's largest lagoon, with hides on its northern shore. Purple Swamphen, Red-crested Pochard and Squacco Heron use it.
    • : The sand spit closing the southern bay. It carries the Audouin's Gull colony and the delta's flamingo flock.
    • : The settlement at the river's mouth, with the beach and the Garxal lagoon beside it for terns and waders.
    • : The flooded rice on the southern bay. Watch from the roads between the paddies for Glossy Ibis and Collared Pratincole.
  • Also covers: Ebro Delta, Els Alfacs rice fields, Encanyissada, Parc Natural del Delta de l'Ebre, Punta de la Banya, Riumar
  • Also watch for: Eurasian Otter has returned to the delta channels, European Pond Turtle basks on the lagoon margins, and the endemic Spanish Toothcarp survives in the brackish pools.

The Aragonese and Catalan steppes

Gypsum and stone steppe on the middle Ebro and the Lleida plains, dry enough to hold Dupont's Lark

Dupont's Lark at the SEO reserves of El Planerón and La Lomaza, with Pin-tailed Sandgrouse, Lesser Short-toed Lark and Black Wheatear. The Lleida plains carry Little Bustard and Montagu's Harrier.

  • Habitat: Gypsum and clay steppe with esparto and low scrub across 40,000 ha, dotted with the seasonal pools that sandgrouse come down to drink at.
  • When: Spring for the steppe birds and early autumn for Dotterel. Dupont's Lark sings at dawn and through the night, so learn the song before you go.
  • Getting there: Belchite is on the A-222, 45 km southeast of Zaragoza. El Planerón is freely open; La Lomaza needs a permit from INAGA, the Aragón environment institute in Zaragoza.
  • Look for: Dupont's Lark, Pin-tailed Sandgrouse, Black-bellied Sandgrouse, Mediterranean Short-toed Lark, Calandra Lark, Montagu's Harrier, Spectacled Warbler
  • Parks and reserves: Reserva Ornitológica El Planerón (SEO/BirdLife reserve), Reserva Natural Dirigida de las Saladas de Chiprana (nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : A reserve of gypsum steppe run for Dupont's Lark. The bird sings before dawn and is heard far more often than it is seen.
    • : The town beside the reserve, with the ruins of the old village left as a memorial. It is the base for a pre-dawn start.
    • : The neighbouring steppe reserve of saltpan and esparto (the tough tussock grass of the dry steppe). Black-bellied Sandgrouse and Calandra Lark hold it.
    • : The semi-desert plateau between Zaragoza and Lleida, and the largest steppe block in western Europe.
    • : Irrigated and dry cereal west of the city, and Catalonia's ground for Little Bustard and Lesser Kestrel.
  • Also covers: Belchite, La Lomaza, Lleida plains, Los Monegros, Reserva Natural Dirigida de las Saladas de Chiprana, Reserva Ornitológica El Planerón
  • Also watch for: Iberian Hare and Red Fox are the mammals of the open steppe. The reptiles are the draw here, with Ocellated Lizard on the gypsum and Montpellier Snake in the scrub.

Gallocanta, the Madrid steppes and Gredos

The largest saline lagoon in Iberia, with the cereal steppe around Madrid and the granite of Gredos on the same leg

Laguna de Gallocanta is the largest saline lagoon in Iberia and eighty per cent of the western Common Crane population passes through it. Single day counts have reached 135,000 cranes. The same central leg takes in the Madrid steppes for Great Bustard and Sierra de Gredos for Bluethroat, Citril Finch and Spanish Imperial Eagle.

  • Habitat: A shallow saline lake at a thousand metres in a cereal basin, with the granite of Guadarrama and Gredos rising above the Madrid plain to the west.
  • When: Cranes arrive from late October and peak in November; the return peaks at the end of February. High summer leaves little water and a formidable heat haze.
  • Getting there: From Zaragoza take the N-330 to Daroca, then the A-211 for 18 km and the CV-633 into Gallocanta village. The Reguera tower hide is reached north from Las Cuerlas.
  • Look for: Common Crane, Bluethroat, Ortolan Bunting, Water Pipit, Rock Sparrow, Northern Wheatear, Iberian Grey Shrike
  • Parks and reserves: Reserva Natural Dirigida de la Laguna de Gallocanta (nature reserve), Parque Nacional de la Sierra de Guadarrama, Parque Regional de la Sierra de Gredos (regional park)
  • Stops:
    • : A shallow salt lake on the Aragonese plateau, and the largest Common Crane staging site in western Europe. Tens of thousands roost on it in autumn.
    • : The village at the lake's northern end, with the interpretation centre. It is the standard place to watch the crane flight at dawn.
    • : The gypsum steppe and river terraces southeast of the capital. Great Bustard live within an hour of the airport.
    • : A granite range west of Madrid with high pasture above the pine. Search it for Bluethroat, Ortolan Bunting and Spanish Ibex.
    • Sierra de Guadarrama National Park : Granite sierra and pine forest an hour north of Madrid. It holds the high-altitude set within reach of the city.
  • Also covers: Bello, Madrid steppes, Parque Nacional de la Sierra de Guadarrama, Parque Regional de la Sierra de Gredos, Reserva Natural Dirigida de la Laguna de Gallocanta, Sierra de Guadarrama National Park
  • Also watch for: Gredos carries the Spanish Ibex subspecies that survived only here, now numerous and approachable in the high circus. Eurasian Otter works the Tormes below, and Iberian Hare holds the cereal plains.

Picos de Europa and the north coast

Limestone massifs rising past 2,600 m within twenty kilometres of the Cantabrian sea

Cantabrian mountains with Wallcreeper, Snowfinch, Alpine Accentor and Capercaillie, and a Bearded Vulture reintroduction running since 2010.

  • Habitat: Limestone massif rising past 2,600 m above beech and oak forest, with the Cantabrian rias and sea cliffs an hour to the north.
  • When: Late May to early July, when the mountain species are at their most visible and most vocal. The rias hold their waders and wildfowl right through the winter.
  • Getting there: Cangas de Onís and Potes are the gateways. The Covadonga lakes road climbs from Cangas and runs a summer shuttle; the Fuente Dé cable car lifts from above Potes.
  • Look for: Western Capercaillie, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, White-backed Woodpecker, Alpine Chough, Ring Ouzel, Yellowhammer, Common Firecrest
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Nacional de los Picos de Europa, Parque Natural de Somiedo (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : A limestone massif rising to 2,600 m within twenty kilometres of the sea. Wallcreeper, Alpine Accentor and Snowfinch hold it.
    • : The cable car at the massif's southern end. It lifts you 750 m to the high karst in four minutes.
    • : A valley system of beech and brañas in Asturias. It is the surest Cantabrian Brown Bear ground and good for Black Woodpecker.
    • : The estuaries of the north coast, sheltered and tidal. Waders use them, with wintering divers and grebes offshore.
  • Also covers: Cantabrian coast, Fuente Dé, Parque Nacional de los Picos de Europa, Parque Natural de Somiedo
  • Also watch for: Cantabrian Brown Bear is recovering in the western massif and Iberian Wolf ranges the same ground. Cantabrian Chamois is reliable on the high limestone and Roe Deer in the beech below.

Albufera, the Levante coast and Mallorca

Coastal lagoons behind the Valencian and Alicante beaches, with Mallorca's own Albufera across the water

The Levante coast holds Albufera de Valencia, which takes up to a hundred species in a migration day, and El Hondo, which holds most of the European Marbled Teal population. Mallorca sits offshore with its own Albufera.

  • Habitat: A freshwater lagoon behind a dune bar with rice paddy on three sides, and a second reed and marsh system at s'Albufera on Mallorca.
  • When: Winter brings the largest waterbird concentrations. The paddies are drained through March, April and October, and shooting disturbs the weekends from November to February.
  • Getting there: The Racó de l'Olla visitor centre is off the CV-500 coast road, 10 km south of Valencia and signposted with El Palmar. S'Albufera is walked in from Ses Puntes at Port d'Alcúdia.
  • Look for: Eleonora's Falcon, Mediterranean Shearwater, Moltoni's Warbler, Eurasian Stone-curlew, Little Tern, Black-necked Grebe, Booted Warbler
  • Parks and reserves: Parc Natural de l'Albufera de València (natural park), Parc Natural de s'Albufera de Mallorca (natural park)
  • Stops:
    • : A freshwater lagoon behind a dune bar with rice fields around it, and the largest wetland on the Levante coast.
    • : Reservoirs and reedbed south of Elche. It holds Marbled Teal and White-headed Duck, both of which are hard anywhere else.
    • : Working saltpans on the coast, with flamingo, Slender-billed Gull and the wader roosts.
    • : The island's great reedbed and marsh behind the Alcudia dunes, with a hide circuit from the visitor centre.
    • : A dry valley walked from Port de Pollença to the sea, and the island's standard site for Balearic Warbler and Eleonora's Falcon.
    • : A walled valley walked from the town to the sea, and the classic Mallorcan migration watch. The Albufereta marsh lies at the other end of the bay.
  • Also covers: El Hondo, Parc Natural de l'Albufera de València, Parc Natural de s'Albufera de Mallorca, Puerto Pollensa and the Boquer valley, Santa Pola
  • Also watch for: Common Genet hunts the pine behind the Valencian lagoons and European Pond Turtle holds the freshwater channels. Mallorca carries the Mallorcan Midwife Toad, which survives in the Tramuntana torrents and nowhere else on earth.

The Catalan coast, from the Empordà to the Llobregat

A Catalan coastal wetland at each end of the Costa Brava, with the rocky headlands and their seabird passage between them

The Aiguamolls de l'Empordà has recorded around 330 species in a compact block of lagoon, reedbed and flooded meadow behind the beach at Roses. The Llobregat delta puts a national hotspot for migrants and rarities twenty minutes from central Barcelona, and Cap de Creus between the two is one of the best places in the Mediterranean to watch seabirds from the shore.

  • Habitat: The Aiguamolls is a compact mosaic of brackish lagoons, freshwater lagoons, reedbed, sand dune, seasonally flooded meadow and riverine woodland between the Fluvià and the Muga. The Llobregat delta is a coastal floodplain of small saline lagoons, dense reedbed, pinewood, saltmarsh and dune. Cap de Creus is a windswept rocky headland of maquis scrub, small pine plantations, holm oak and olive groves.
  • When: March to May and August to October for the passage, which is when both wetlands are at their best. Little Crake is more reliable at the Aiguamolls in spring than anywhere else in Spain, and wintering Mediterranean Gull counts at the Llobregat sometimes pass 10,000 birds.
  • Getting there: Take the AP-7 or the N-II to Figueres, then the C-68 towards Castelló d'Empúries and the GI-6216 towards Sant Pere Pescador. The Aiguamolls visitors' centre is signposted on the left after about 3 km. For the Llobregat delta leave Barcelona on the C-31 towards El Prat de Llobregat and take the Remolar-Filipines exit, which is the last one before Airport T-1.
  • Look for: Audouin's Gull, Purple Swamphen, Little Crake, Moustached Warbler, Eurasian Bittern, Mediterranean Gull, Alpine Accentor, Wallcreeper
  • Parks and reserves: Parc Natural dels Aiguamolls de l'Empordà (natural park), Parc Natural de Cap de Creus (natural park), Reserva Natural del Remolar-Filipines (nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : This is the core of the Aiguamolls. The visitors' centre stands here, and marked trails run out to hides over the brackish lagoons and the grazed meadows.
    • : A hide overlooks this freshwater lagoon at the northern end of the reserve, beyond the Empuriabrava holiday complex.
    • : The Fluvià runs past the village between willow, poplar, alder and tamarisk. Golden Oriole and Nightingale sing along the river in spring.
    • : This rocky headland is the easternmost point of mainland Spain. Thousands of Yelkouan Shearwaters feed off it on the anchovy shoals in December and January.
    • : The monastery and the peak of Sant Salvador above it hold the park office. Alpine Accentor and Wallcreeper come down from the Pyrenees to winter on the walls and the boulders.
    • : This is the accessible half of the Llobregat delta. A small information centre, a path circuit and several hides cover the lagoons, and a tower on the beach looks out over the sea.
  • Also covers: Castelló d'Empúries, El Cortalet, El Prat de Llobregat, Estany de Vilaüt, Parc Natural de Cap de Creus, Parc Natural dels Aiguamolls de l'Empordà, Reserva Natural del Remolar-Filipines, Sant Pere de Rodes, Sant Pere Pescador, Viladecans
  • Also watch for: Cattle and Camargue horses graze the old rice fields at the Aiguamolls, and Eurasian Otter and Fallow Deer have both been reintroduced there. European Polecat, Marbled Newt and Mediterranean Terrapin live in the channels.

La Mancha, Daimiel and the Húmeda lagoons

The smallest national park in Spain, set in a plain of a hundred shallow salt lagoons under the windmills of La Mancha

Las Tablas de Daimiel is the last of the river washes that once flooded much of the Castilian plain, and it holds over 100 pairs of Purple Heron and a clamorous Common Crane roost on winter evenings. The hundred seasonal lagoons of La Mancha Húmeda around it carry one of the largest breeding populations of Black-necked Grebe in Europe.

  • Habitat: Las Tablas is a maze of islands, channels and shallow flooded land at the meeting of the brackish Cigüela and the Guadiana, with wide tracts of reedbed and open water and tamarisk as its only tree. The lagoons of La Mancha Húmeda are shallow seasonal waters on saline soils, most of them small, ringed by cereal, vines and irrigated sunflowers.
  • When: Any month outside June to October, because most of the lagoons dry out through the summer. Winter brings the cranes and up to 10,000 ducks to Daimiel, and late March and April carry the best of the wader passage.
  • Getting there: Las Tablas lies about 140 km from Madrid and 40 km from Ciudad Real. Leave the A-4 at Manzanares and take the A-43 west for 22 km to Daimiel, where the park is signposted from the bypass road and sits 11 km further along a tarmac road. The lagoons of La Mancha Húmeda lie around Alcázar de San Juan, 30 km east of the A-4 at Madridejos on the CM-42.
  • Look for: Black-necked Grebe, White-headed Duck, Red-crested Pochard, Marbled Duck, Bearded Reedling, Moustached Warbler, Great Bustard, Common Crane
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Parque Nacional de Las Tablas de Daimiel
    • Reserva Natural de la Laguna de Manjavacas (nature reserve)
    • Los Charcones de Miguel Esteban (SEO/BirdLife reserve), SEO/BirdLife holds a reserve on these lagoons. The muddy shores take passage waders, and the cereal around them carries Great Bustard and Pin-tailed Sandgrouse.
  • Stops:
    • : Three colour-coded trails run on footpaths and boardwalks across reedbed and open water to hides over the mixed heronries. The visitors' centre lies 11 km from the Daimiel bypass.
    • : This restored lagoon beside the water treatment works north of Daimiel town gives the closest views of any site here, and it holds waders and wildfowl when the park itself runs low.
    • : Manjavacas usually keeps water through the summer, so Black-necked Grebe and Gull-billed Tern gather here in July. Greater Flamingo visits and has nested.
    • : The town sits at the centre of the lagoon complex and its own Ramsar lagoons lie on its edge, which makes it the practical base for working the group.
    • : The Vega del Pueblo lagoon at Pedro Muñoz is a Ramsar site and a nature reserve, and its salty margins are among the better wader shores in autumn.
  • Also covers: Alcázar de San Juan, Laguna de Navaseca, Laguna de Pedro Muñoz, Los Charcones de Miguel Esteban, Parque Nacional de Las Tablas de Daimiel, Reserva Natural de la Laguna de Manjavacas
  • Also watch for: Eurasian Otter and European Polecat work the channels at Las Tablas, and Wild Boar, Red Fox, Least Weasel and Garden Dormouse live in the reedbed and the tamarisk. European Pond Turtle and Spanish Terrapin bask on the margins.

Sierra Nevada, Cabo de Gata and the Almería steppe

The highest ground in Spain above the driest corner of Europe, with alpine tops, working salt pans and true steppe within one day's drive

Mulhacén and Pico Veleta hold the most southerly breeding Alpine Accentors in Iberia along with Citril Finch and Ortolan Bunting, and a road climbs to 2,500 m from Granada. Two hours east, Cabo de Gata takes about 200 mm of rain a year, the lowest in Europe, and its salt pans, steppe and semi-desert hold Trumpeter Finch, Dupont's Lark and hundreds of Greater Flamingos.

  • Habitat: The Sierra Nevada rises through Scots and Black Pine woodland to spiny hedgehog scrub at 1,700 to 2,000 m, dwarf juniper to about 2,600 m, and alpine moorland and stony scree above that. The Almería lowlands hold working salt pans, xerophytic scrub, dune and open steppe, and the Tabernas badlands are eroded ramblas with stands of tamarisk in their beds.
  • When: April to June for the high tops, once the road above Granada is clear. March to late May and late August to October are best on the salt pans, and the steppe and the sierra reward early mornings and late evenings from March onwards.
  • Getting there: The A-395 climbs 45 km from Granada city to the ski station at 2,500 m, and the main visitors' centre, El Dornajo, sits at km 26 on that road. For Almería take the A-7 along the coast, then the AL-3115 from the roundabout west of Ruescas for the Cabo de Gata salt pans, where a lay-by and several hides overlook the lagoon.
  • Look for: Alpine Accentor, Citril Finch, Trumpeter Finch, Dupont's Lark, Black Wheatear, Audouin's Gull, Greater Flamingo, Black-bellied Sandgrouse
  • Parks and reserves: Parque Nacional de Sierra Nevada, Parque Natural de Cabo de Gata-Níjar (natural park), Paraje Natural de Punta Entinas-Sabinar (nature reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : A minibus runs from the Albergue Universitario to the Mirador del Veleta at 3,100 m in summer, which is the easy way onto the alpine zone. Alpine Accentor, Northern Wheatear and Black Redstart breed on the summit plateau.
    • : The main Sierra Nevada visitors' centre stands at km 26 on the A-395 from Granada, and the pine and scrub around it hold Citril Finch and Iberian Green Woodpecker.
    • : This pass crosses the eastern end of the range at 2,000 m. The Citril Finches of the Sierra Nevada are easiest here, and tracks run north and south off the road.
    • : These are the only working salt pans left in Almería. Several hundred Greater Flamingos are usually present, and Audouin's Gull loafs here in numbers in late summer.
    • : The dune and steppe west of the cape is the most productive dry ground in the park, and the park visitors' centre stands beside it at km 7 on the AL-3115.
    • : Signposted trails run into the dry ramblas from the tourist office on the N-340a beside Tabernas. Trumpeter Finch, Black Wheatear, Dupont's Lark and Black-bellied Sandgrouse all use this ground.
    • : A 6.5 km trail runs west from the car park at the end of Almerimar past seasonal lagoons in fixed dune. It is one of the best stretches of this coast for waders and terns.
  • Also covers: Almería, Desierto de Tabernas, El Dornajo, Granada, Las Amoladeras, Paraje Natural de Punta Entinas-Sabinar, Parque Nacional de Sierra Nevada, Parque Natural de Cabo de Gata-Níjar, Pico Veleta, Puerto de la Ragua, Salinas de Cabo de Gata
  • Also watch for: Spanish Ibex grazes the high slopes of the Sierra Nevada in good numbers, and the sheep flocks share the ground with it. The range carries the highest density of endemic plants anywhere in Europe and the Mediterranean basin, and 40 of them grow above 2,600 m.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Spain?

March and April, if you want one answer. The bustards are displaying, the steppes are still green, Extremadura's vultures are on the nest and Doñana is on passage. Late August and early September is the other answer, for the raptor crossing at the Strait of Gibraltar, and November to February for the cranes and the lynx.

Where should I go first?

Extremadura and Doñana together, which is how nearly every operator sells the first Spanish trip. Four nights on the marsh and four on the steppe, with Monfragüe in between, covers the vultures, the bustards, the Imperial Eagle and the Iberian Magpie.

Can I drive into Doñana?

Not into the interior. Guided four wheel drive tours of about twenty-one seats run from the El Acebuche visitor centre and need booking ahead, at roughly twenty-five to forty euros a head, with a shorter authorised route from El Rocío. The visitor centres themselves have hides and walking trails you can use freely.

Is Doñana still worth going to, given the drought?

Yes, and go knowing what you are looking at. Every lagoon including Santa Olalla dried out completely in the summers of 2022 and 2023, groundwater near the marsh has fallen by as much as twenty metres, and recorded marsh biodiversity fell from 4.3 species per square kilometre in 2003 to 2.5 in 2021. The cause is drought compounded by extraction for strawberry farming in Huelva, and UNESCO has warned about the World Heritage listing. Winter and spring still hold enormous numbers. Summer is a different and much thinner place than the reputation suggests.

How reliable is the Tarifa raptor migration?

Reliable across a week, unreliable on any given day, because the crossing depends on wind. Roughly three hundred thousand raptors of about thirty species and a hundred and fifty thousand storks pass each season, and the peak is the last week of August into the first ten days of September. Give it several days rather than one.

What are my chances of seeing an Iberian Lynx?

Better than they have been in living memory, and still a matter of patience. The population has gone from about a hundred animals in 2002 to about 2,400 in 2024, and the Sierra de Andújar holds the densest concentration. Winter is the season, when coats are short and the cover is thin.

Why does this guide list no places to stay yet?

Because Spain runs on different schemes from the northern European guides. Green Key has twelve currently awarded properties in the whole country. Spain uses Biosphere, whose register holds 3,384 certified businesses, and the European Charter for Sustainable Tourism inside its national parks, alongside Travelife, EarthCheck and Green Globe. Every property listed here holds one of those and sits within about forty-five kilometres of somewhere in the regions above.

How hot does it actually get?

Hot enough to change the trip. August in Monfragüe regularly passes forty degrees, and the guides who work there describe it as an endurance exercise. From June to September in the south, birding happens between first light and about ten, then again in the last two hours, and the middle of the day belongs to shade.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Sites on this page differ from each other more than any rating could carry, so this is the framework the standard British guides use, and the reserve's own page and warden hold the answers.

  • Permission · some reserves open ground to disabled visitors that is closed to everyone else, and it is granted by asking.
  • Priority · parking bays, hides and the nearest paths are often held for disabled visitors. Ask what is reserved and how to claim it.
  • Parking · how close a car reaches the birds shapes the whole day. Ring ahead for the nearest hard standing to the water or the hide.
  • Paths · surfaces, gradients and gate widths vary inside a single reserve. Ask which trail is boarded, surfaced or level.
  • Perches · a hide with a low window, or a bench where the view opens, turns a viewpoint into a morning.

Every reserve above with its own link carries its access detail there, and a warden answers what a page cannot.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, Spain has 27 local bird clubs across 17 regions. See every Spanish club by region.

SEO/BirdLife The BirdLife partner, founded in 1954 with around eight thousand members. It owns the Belchite reserves that hold Dupont's Lark. Visit Comité de Rarezas de SEO/BirdLife The rarities committee. It has run since 1984 and is Spain's representative to the European records committees, and its annual report appears in Ardeola. Visit Ardeola SEO/BirdLife's scientific journal, and where the Spanish rarities reports are published. Visit FIO The international birding tourism fair. It is held inside Monfragüe each winter, and the 2026 edition was its twenty-first and drew over 121 exhibitors. Visit
